en: His heart is steel, his outer frame is bronze—
What man could ever stand against him?
When fury seizes and maddens him,
He darts like ten striking snakes;
His combat blazes like red-hot coals—
What wrestler could withstand him?
Would anyone dare face him in battle?
Would anyone he attacks remain alive?
When enraged, he cannot be restrained;
No man he pursues can escape.
My bosom friend, listen to my words:
The two reins and the single bridle—
I yield them to you, my friend; take command.
Against this hero raging in fury,
You yourself must wage the battle.
This handful of the Jediger—
Would there be sin or merit in destroying them?
Take the duty upon yourself;
Hero, wage the battle yourself.
He is the enemy whose secrets you know;
My friend, deal with him as you know best.
Hero, do not stir up
Any needless quarrel.
My lion, whose cunning is complete,
Devise the means to deal with him yourself.
The Jediger will face a true slaughter—
Hero, bind him with your own hands.
Your hero’s courage is unmatched, his venom fierce;
If you do not act as you see fit,
My dearest friend,
He will level every one of us.
If you mean to kill him, kill him yourself;
Hero, if you mean to bind him, bind him yourself!
Hero, use all your cunning.
Do not think I shrink from combat;
Hero, restrain your anger.
Here stand the Kyrgyz people with their chiefs;
If you would cut off my head, here I stand.
This slave of yours has driven me into a frenzy;
Hero, if you would kill me, here is the ground.
Hero, if you are enraged, here is your chance.
Let me offer before you
This fleet bay racehorse as a gift.
Hero, if you bear a grudge, here are my people;
If you would sever my head,
Here am I, your precious Kyyaz!
Hero, as Kanchoro you have prospered—
Külchoro and Kanchoro,
You two grew up as equals.
You are confidants raised side by side;
Hero, you are comrades of the same age.
Spear him as you see fit;
Hero, bind your enemy.
These teeming black-clad Jediger—
I will not contest them with you;
Take their khanship for yourself.
Hero, do whatever the occasion demands.
Hero, Kanchoro and Külchoro,
You are confidants who grew up together;
United when you were no bigger than lice,
Joined when you were no bigger than thumbs.
Your sheep shared the same fold,
Your heads shared the same fellowship;
Whatever you found, you gathered together.
I know the hero’s secret—
Spear him yourself!”
So spoke brave Kyyaz;
Terrified by the hero’s venom,
Brave Kyyaz stood in anguish,
Pleading with Kanchoro.
When Kanchoro heard this,
He bristled in wrath,
Swelling boldly with resolve;
His eyes gaped like an opened pit,
His face gleamed like oiled wheat.
His two cheeks hung loose,
Enough to feast two giants;
When the savage grew enraged,
He seemed ready to slaughter anyone he fought.
With a steel haft and a keen edge,
He strapped on his battle-axe,
Put on his arrow-proof coat,
And his hostile intent became plain.
That broad-jawed battle-axe,
Its steel edge honed sharp,
Its handle wound with gold,
Destined for the enemy he would fight,
Was fashioned in every splendid form
By the master of masters, the great smith,
By Bölökbay himself.
When it came time to temper it,
The waters of the Black Spring were drained;
The smith perfected its edge.
Unable to supply enough charcoal,
A forest of plane trees was destroyed;
No creature could endure the bellows’ demands,
So a blue bull was slaughtered.
Such was the battle-axe.
He slipped it over his bare forearm;
Look closely, and Kanchoro
Raged like a white tiger,
Growling and working himself into fury.
The wretch strode forth
And addressed Külchoro.
But poor Külchoro
Had no strength left to exchange blows,
No means left there to wrestle,
No power left to grapple.
All strength had deserted the hero;
He stood there in angry anguish,
The poor man,
Pleading with Kanchoro:
“Oh, my dear Kanchoro,
You have known me from our earliest days—
My warrior who took the socketed spear
And shattered armies beyond number!
Today, elder brother and khan,
I am a wretch fallen into your hands.
Like grass swept into a wildfire,
Robbed of every protector,
I bow my neck to death.
We were foster brothers from the beginning;
My lord, I stand in your hands.
Hero, if you stiffen in wrath,
I will not resist—slaughter me.
Yet if we truly were foster brothers,
Spare me and leave me alive.
Were we not slopes upon the same mountain pass,
Foster brothers sharing a single soul?
Whatever we found, we gathered together;
We grew up together, companions of one age.
We kicked and tussled like colt and yearling,
And quarreled as we suckled the same breast.
We slept in the same bed
And shared the same delights.
We gathered our allotted herds together,
And grew like twins, companions of one age.”
Thus he spoke these words,
And Külchoro stood in anguish.
Kanchoro, that once-noble hero,
Stood enraged and ready;
No pleading could save a life.
He would destroy everything there was—
Kanchoro the khan felt no regret.
Its steel haft was thick as a fist:
Such was the battle-axe.
His waist sagging, his back bent,
His eyes rolling and bulging,
He gripped his black-steel axe
In both hands and swung it round.
Kanchoro gathered all his fury:
“The cleft of his shoulder blades is the spot—
Here is where this raging false slave
Shall meet his death!”
He seized his blood-drinking axe
And swung it round;
He charged the hero
And struck at the nape of his neck.
Then, shouting in rage,
“Surround and bind him, wrestlers!”
He summoned his champions,
And Kanchoro stood facing him.
As Kanchoro confronted him,
The peerlessly agile,
Clashing lion-hero,
The merciless warrior who had subdued the world,
Stood ready.
Yesterday, while leopard Manas yet lived,
A wondrous blade had come to him by fate
From the heights of the Mediyan Desert,
From a sheer ridge facing the traveler,
From a crag where mountains vanished,
From the jutting brow of a stooping peak:
The Six-Edged Blade that fell from heaven,
The finest and most deadly of swords,
The strongest of living steel.
When drawn from its sheath with a battle cry,
It never went idle without drinking blood;
Until it had drunk its fill of blood,
It would not return to its sheath.
Laid upon grass, it kindled fire;
Whoever it marked was swiftly destroyed.
Drawn from its sheath, it glowed red;
When swung at the foe with a cry,
It lengthened to forty fathoms.
The renowned Six-Edged Blade—
Külchoro grasped its scabbard,
Drew it by the hilt,
And before Kanchoro could pull back,
The ever-ready Külchoro
Had the sword in hand.
Before Kanchoro could twist away,
Turn and draw back,
Külchoro flared in rage;
He caught the slave upright
By the bottom hem.
The falcon warrior drew the blade crosswise
And stood brandishing it;
The slave’s right coat-tail
He sliced clean away.
One thigh of Akborchuk
He hewed through to the bone,
And one thigh of Kökborchuk
He hewed through to the bone.
Before the hero could recover,
Before he could wreak destruction upon them,
The teeming black-clad Jediger
And bloodthirsty lion, brave Kyyaz,
Fell upon the hero.
Their toughest veteran wrestlers,
Every one of their champions,
Raised shouts from every side;
From all directions
They cried their battle cry, “Kıyır!”
They loosed their bows like pouring rain,
Shooting volleys of many kinds.
The arrows from bows hissed,
The musket balls shrieked,
The cannon shot thundered;
Now they waged a boundless battle.
The ever-ready hero
Spent all his strength and lost his power;
Dark blood poured from his body,
And Külchoro’s strength ebbed away.
The peerless warrior’s two arms
Could no longer rise and hung paralyzed;
His breast filled with black blood.
He had no swift steed to bear him away,
No kinsman in that land to lead him home.
Alone amid the Jediger host—
Such, indeed, is this worthless world.
The great pit dug for him
Now began to boil with misery.
Thrusting spears and striking axes,
They engulfed him there.
Those armed with ropes and armored coats,
All the men with iron gauntlets,
The champions who thrust spears,
The heroes who struck with battle-axes,
Those most skilled with swords,
The strongest of the mighty,
Surrounded him.
On that occasion, the hero
Passed through desperate torment;
The Jediger ringed him round
And cast him into a net of iron.
Over poor Külchoro,
The heroes Kanchoro and Kyyaz
Stiffened in wrath,
Roared in harsh fury,
Thundered in anger,
And growled like lions.
At the sight of their terrible bearing,
Men’s bodies trembled;
Their courage was like a wild boar’s rage,
Like creatures that would leave nothing alive.
